Patient Information

Balance and Strength at Home

A home programme to steady your balance and reduce your risk of falling — no equipment, no gym, ten to twenty minutes a day.

Feeling less steady than you used to is one of the most common reasons people are sent to see me, and one of the most treatable. Balance is not a fixed quality you are born with and gradually lose. It is a skill, built from leg strength, the sensation in your feet, your inner ear, your vision and your reaction speed — and like any skill, it improves with the right practice.

The programme below is the one I give my own patients. It uses nothing but a kitchen bench, a firm chair and a corridor. What matters is not which exercises you choose but two things the research is unusually clear about: the balance work has to feel slightly wobbly, and you have to do enough of it.

The single most important sentence on this page

Exercise that never makes you feel slightly unsteady does not reduce falls. That is why every exercise here comes with a way to make it harder — and a bench to hold on to while you do.

How to use this sheet
  • Read it once through, then start with the first two or three exercises only.
  • Add an exercise every week or two rather than starting everything at once.
  • Print it, tick off the days, and bring it back to your appointment.
  • This sheet is general information for my patients. If you have been given different, specific advice about your own condition, that advice comes first.
Before you start — making this safe to do alone
  • Always have something solid to grab. A kitchen bench, a heavy table, a wall on each side, or the back of a chair wedged against a wall. Not a wheeled chair, not a towel rail.
  • Choose the right floor. Bare, level, non-slip. Move rugs and cords out of the way. Do not do balance work on a rug edge or a wet bathroom floor.
  • Wear shoes or bare feet, not socks. Well-fitting shoes with a firm heel counter and a thin sole let you feel the floor.
  • If you have fallen in the last six months, or you feel unsafe standing still with your feet together, do not start alone. Do these first with a family member present, or ask me to arrange a physiotherapist.
  • Carry your phone, or wear a personal alarm, if you live alone.
  • Stop and contact your doctor if an exercise causes chest pain, sudden severe dizziness, a new weakness, or a fall.

What actually makes balance training work

Three ingredients separate the programmes that reduced falls in trials from the ones that did nothing at all.

👣 Narrow your base

Feet apart is easy. Feet together is harder. One foot in front of the other is harder again. One leg is hardest. Every session should spend time at the edge of what you can hold.

🤸 Move your weight around

Standing still is only half of balance. Reaching, leaning, turning and stepping — moving your centre of gravity and bringing it back under control — is the other half, and it is what real life demands.

✋ Let go of your hands

Two hands gripping the bench does very little for your balance. The training happens as you progress to one hand, then a fingertip, then a hand hovering ready to catch you.

The arithmetic that decides whether this works

Across the trials, the programmes that halved falls delivered around three hours a week and about fifty hours in total — that is roughly four to six months of consistent practice. Three short sessions a week comes to about ninety minutes: good, but below the threshold. The way to close that gap is not another formal session you will not do. It is to scatter balance into the day: stand on one leg while the kettle boils, do five sit-to-stands in every ad break, walk sideways along the bench between the fridge and the sink, and stand in tandem while you clean your teeth. That approach was tested on its own and reduced falls by about a third, with better adherence than a structured programme.

Part 1 — Strength

Three days a week, on non-consecutive days. Strength is what gives you something to balance with.

Chair squats (sit-to-stand)

10 repetitions × 2–3 sets, 3 days a week
Highest-value exercise

The single most useful strengthening exercise for an older adult: it is how you get off the toilet, out of the car, and up off the floor after a fall.

  1. Use a firm dining chair with its back against a wall. Not an armchair, not a chair on castors.
  2. Sit forward on the seat with your feet flat, hip-width apart, drawn back slightly so your heels sit under your knees.
  3. Lean your chest forwards over your knees (nose over toes) — this, not leg strength, is what most people are missing.
  4. Push down through your heels and stand up all the way, squeezing your buttocks at the top.
  5. Lower yourself back down slowly — take 3 seconds — and touch the seat lightly rather than dropping onto it.
  6. That is one repetition. Do 10, rest a minute, and repeat.
Make it harderArms folded across the chest instead of pushing off your knees. Then a slower, 4-second lowering. Then a lower seat (a firm cushion removed, or a lower chair). Then stand from the chair and hold a half-squat for 3 seconds before sitting.
Make it easierPush off your thighs or the chair arms with your hands, and use a higher seat with a cushion on it. Even five repetitions counts.
SafetyChair against a wall, every time. If your knees are painful, reduce the depth rather than abandoning the exercise.
Why it worksSit-to-stand is a named component of the Otago programme — which reduced falls by about a third in trials of frail older people with an average age of 81 — and functional balance training of this kind carries a strong recommendation in the 2022 World Guidelines for Falls Prevention.

Standing leg raises — front, side and back

10 raises in each of the 3 directions, each leg, 3 days a week
Strength + balance in one

Strengthens the hip muscles (particularly the side-hip muscles that stop your pelvis dropping) while forcing you to balance on the other leg. Two exercises for the price of one.

  1. Stand tall behind a firm chair or at the bench, hands resting on it.
  2. Front: keeping the knee straight and the body upright, lift one leg forward about 20–30 cm. Lower slowly under control. Repeat 10 times.
  3. Side: lift the same leg directly out to the side, toes pointing forwards (not turned out), 20–30 cm. Do not lean away — the trick is to keep your trunk vertical. Lower slowly. Repeat 10 times.
  4. Back: lift the leg straight behind you, squeezing the buttock, without arching your low back or leaning forwards. Repeat 10 times.
  5. Swap legs and repeat all three directions.
Make it harderReduce hand support to fingertips. Then add a 2-second hold at the top of each raise. Then add a light ankle weight (start at 0.5–1 kg) for the side and back raises.
Make it easierDo them seated for the front raises, and do side and back raises with both hands firmly on the bench and a smaller range.
SafetySlow and controlled beats high. A 20 cm raise done with a still trunk builds far more than a 50 cm raise done by swinging and leaning.
Why it worksAnkle-weighted hip and knee exercises are the strength backbone of the Otago programme, which cut falls by roughly a third (rate ratio 0.68) across seven trials, and which also reduced falls in people referred to a falls clinic after an injury.

Heel raises (calf strength)

10–15 repetitions × 2 sets, 3 days a week
Otago exercise

The calf is the engine of push-off in walking and the first muscle that catches you when you sway forwards.

  1. Stand at the bench, feet hip-width apart, hands resting on it for balance only.
  2. Rise up onto the balls of both feet as high as you can.
  3. Pause for a second at the top — most people cheat this part.
  4. Lower slowly, taking about 3 seconds, until your heels touch the floor.
  5. Repeat 10 to 15 times.
Make it harderFingertip support only. Then single-leg heel raises (holding the bench), building to 10 each side. Then do them with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step so the heel drops below the step — only with a solid rail.
Make it easierSmaller range, both hands on the bench, and do them seated first if standing is unsteady.
SafetyIf you get calf cramps, reduce the number and stretch afterwards. Stop if you get sudden calf pain and swelling — that needs assessment.
Why it worksCalf strength and ankle power decline steeply with age and correlate closely with walking speed, which itself predicts falls, hospitalisation and independence.

Toe raises (shin strength)

10–15 repetitions × 2 sets, 3 days a week
Otago exercise

The muscles on the front of the shin lift your toes clear of the carpet. When they are weak, you trip.

  1. Stand at the bench with your feet hip-width apart.
  2. Keeping your heels planted, lift the fronts of both feet up as far as you can.
  3. Hold for a second, then lower slowly.
  4. Repeat 10 to 15 times.
Make it harderDo them one foot at a time, or while standing on one leg with support.
Make it easierDo them sitting in a chair with your heels on the floor.
SafetyDo not lean back on the bench to make it easier — keep your weight over your feet.
Why it worksWeak ankle dorsiflexors are strongly associated with trips, which are the most common single mechanism of falls in people who are still walking independently.

Step-ups on the bottom stair

10 step-ups each leg, 2 sets, 3 days a week
Power + confidence

Rebuilds the leg power you need for stairs, kerbs and buses, and rehearses the exact task people become frightened of.

  1. Use the bottom step of a staircase with a solid handrail, or a sturdy step block.
  2. Hold the rail. Place one whole foot on the step.
  3. Push down through that heel to lift yourself up — try to let the leg on the step do the work rather than pushing off the floor with the back foot.
  4. Step back down slowly, leading with the same leg, and touch down quietly.
  5. Do 10 with that leg, then swap.
Make it harderLight fingertip contact on the rail; then a slower 3-second lowering; then a higher step (only with a rail).
Make it easierA single low step or a thick book taped down; or start by simply stepping up and down onto a doorway threshold.
SafetyHandrail in hand for every repetition until you are certain. Shoes on.
Why it worksStair negotiation demands more strength than walking and is where a lot of serious falls occur, so it is worth training deliberately rather than avoiding.

Part 2 — Balance

Most days. This is the part that reduces falls, and the part people skip.

Weight shifts and reaching

10 shifts in each direction, daily
Starting point

Teaches you where your limits of balance actually are, and how to move to the edge of them and come back without panicking.

  1. Stand at the bench, feet hip-width apart, hands lightly resting on it.
  2. Keeping your body straight like a tall mast, sway slowly forwards over your toes, then back over your heels. Go only as far as you can come back from.
  3. Do ten of those, then sway slowly side to side, taking your weight over one foot then the other, ten times.
  4. Then reach one hand slowly out to the side and across your body, following your hand with your eyes, and return.
  5. Finish by reaching down towards a spot on the floor beside your foot and back up.
Make it harderReduce hand support; increase how far you reach; reach to place and pick up an object on a low stool.
Make it easierDo it seated on a firm chair first, or with both hands on the bench and very small movements.
SafetySmall ranges first. The point is control, not distance.
Why it worksReaching while standing is one of the functional balance tasks named in the 2022 World Falls Guidelines, and it directly rehearses the movements that cause household falls.

Tandem and semi-tandem standing

3 × 30 seconds each foot in front, daily
Foundation

The static version of tandem walking — the safest way to start if walking heel-to-toe is still too much.

  1. Stand beside a kitchen bench with one hand resting on it.
  2. Put one foot half a step in front of the other, heel beside the opposite big toe (semi-tandem).
  3. Hold for 30 seconds, breathing normally, eyes ahead.
  4. Swap which foot is in front and repeat.
  5. When 30 seconds is comfortable, move the front foot fully in front (true tandem) so heel touches toe.
Make it harderOne fingertip on the bench, then no hands, then eyes closed with a hand hovering over the bench — eyes closed doubles the difficulty and is where the real gains are.
Make it easierFeet together, both hands on the bench, 30 seconds.
SafetyStand facing into the corner of a bench, not out into the room, so there is something to catch on either side.
Why it worksFeet-together, semi-tandem and tandem stance are the standard progression used in the Otago programme and in nearly every trial that reduced falls.

Single-leg standing

Build to 30 seconds each leg, 2 rounds, daily
Otago exercise

Almost every step you take is a moment of standing on one leg. This trains the hip and ankle muscles that stop you toppling sideways.

  1. Stand at the bench with both hands on it.
  2. Shift your weight fully onto one leg and lift the other foot a few centimetres off the floor — just enough to clear it.
  3. Keep the standing knee soft, hips level, and look at a fixed point ahead.
  4. Hold as long as you can steadily, up to 30 seconds, then swap.
  5. Do two rounds on each leg.
Make it harderTwo fingers on the bench → one finger → hands hovering just above it. Then add slow head turns, or stand on a firm cushion.
Make it easierKeep the toes of the lifted foot resting lightly on the floor (a 'kickstand'), taking almost no weight.
SafetyAlways within arm's reach of support. Do not test yourself in the middle of the room to 'see how long you can last'.
Why it worksSingle-leg stance time is one of the balance tests used to decide who needs a falls intervention. Being unable to hold it for 10 seconds is a marker worth telling me about — it has been linked to higher mortality and to injurious falls, though it is a warning light rather than a target in itself.

Tandem walking (heel-to-toe), corridor only

10 steps × 3, once a day
Core balance drill

Trains the side-to-side balance control that keeps you upright when you turn, step around something, or are jostled.

  1. Do this in a corridor narrow enough that you can touch both walls with your elbows out, or beside a kitchen bench. Never in the middle of a room.
  2. Stand at one end with your fingertips lightly brushing one wall.
  3. Place one foot directly in front of the other so the heel of the front foot touches the toes of the back foot, as if walking a tightrope.
  4. Take ten slow heel-to-toe steps, looking ahead at a point on the wall rather than at your feet.
  5. Turn around carefully — wide, slow steps, not a quick pivot — and walk back.
  6. Rest, then repeat twice more.
Make it harderFingertips off the wall (but still within reach). Then hands folded across your chest. Then walk backwards heel-to-toe. Only when all of that is easy, try it with your head turning slowly side to side.
Make it easierWalk with one whole hand on the wall, and use a semi-tandem step (front heel beside the back toes, not in front of them) until that feels steady.
SafetyNever in an open room, never on a rug, never in socks. If you find yourself repeatedly grabbing the wall, the drill is too hard — go back a stage.
Why it worksNarrowing your base of support is the most efficient way to challenge balance, and challenging balance is what makes falls prevention work. In the Cochrane review of 108 trials, exercise reduced the rate of falls by 23% overall — but programmes that genuinely challenged balance and totalled three or more hours a week reduced falls by around 40%. Comfortable, seated, low-dose programmes did not.

Sideways and backward walking

10 steps each way × 2, most days
Direction training

Most falls happen when you step sideways or backwards — reaching into a cupboard, stepping back from an open door, being nudged. Practise the directions you actually fall in.

  1. Stand side-on to the kitchen bench with one hand on it.
  2. Step sideways along the bench: step out with the leading foot, then bring the trailing foot to meet it. Ten steps.
  3. Come back the other way, so both directions are trained.
  4. Then, facing the bench with both hands on it, take ten slow steps backwards and ten forwards along its length.
  5. Keep your steps deliberate and your body upright.
Make it harderCross-over stepping (grapevine) sideways; fingertip support only; then a slightly quicker tempo.
Make it easierTwo hands on the bench and half-sized steps.
SafetyLook behind you before backward stepping, and keep the path completely clear. Never reverse into an open room.
Why it worksStepping and walking in different directions and at different speeds is specifically recommended in the 2022 World Falls Guidelines, because balance training is task-specific: practising forwards walking does not protect you sideways.

Walking with head turns

3 lengths of the corridor, most days
Real-world balance

Balance fails when you have to look away from where you are going — checking traffic, reading a shelf, being spoken to. This trains that exact situation safely.

  1. Walk down a clear corridor at your normal pace, within reach of a wall.
  2. As you walk, turn your head slowly to the left, count two steps, then slowly to the right, count two steps. Keep walking in a straight line.
  3. Do one length with side-to-side head turns, then one length nodding up and down.
  4. If you feel dizzy or you veer, stop, steady yourself, and make the head movements slower and smaller.
Make it harderFaster head turns, then adding a task — naming animals, counting backwards from 100 by threes — while you walk.
Make it easierDo the head turns standing still with a hand on the bench before combining them with walking.
SafetyCorridor only. If head turning provokes true spinning vertigo rather than mild unsteadiness, stop and tell me — that is a different problem.
Why it worksHead movement removes visual stabilisation and forces the inner ear and body-position senses to do the work. Dual-task walking training is specifically recommended in the 2022 World Falls Guidelines.

Part 3 — The background

Walking will not prevent falls on its own — but everything else works better on top of it.

Walking — the background to everything else

Build towards 30 minutes on most days
Aerobic base

Walking will not by itself fix your balance, but it maintains leg strength, bone, mood, sleep and blood pressure control, and it is the platform the rest of the programme sits on.

  1. Start from where you actually are. If that is five minutes to the letterbox and back, start there.
  2. Add roughly 10% per week — an extra two or three minutes.
  3. Walk at a pace where you could talk but not sing.
  4. Take a route you can shorten easily if you tire: laps of a level block beat a one-way walk you have to complete.
  5. If you are unsteady, walk with someone, or use walking poles or your stick — using an aid is not a failure, it is what allows you to do more.
Make it harderAdd a hill, add pace intervals (two minutes brisk, two minutes easy), or add uneven ground such as a grassy park — but only once your balance work is solid.
Make it easierSplit it into three 10-minute walks. Indoor shopping-centre laps are a legitimate winter option.
SafetyDo not do your balance-challenging exercises outdoors on uneven ground unsupervised.
Why it worksBe clear about this: walking alone has not been shown to prevent falls, and across 88 trials the programmes that included walking training had smaller effects on falls than those that did not. Walking is essential for fitness, mood, bone and nerve health. It is not a substitute for the balance work above.

Putting it together — a week that works

Adapt the days to suit yourself. Keep the structure: strength three times, balance most days, walking on the days between.

DayMain session (20–30 min)Scattered through the day
MondayStrength: chair squats, leg raises, heel and toe raises, step-upsTandem stance at the sink · one-leg stand at the kettle
TuesdayWalk 20–30 minutes5 sit-to-stands each ad break
WednesdayBalance: weight shifts, tandem stance, single-leg, corridor tandem walkingSideways walking along the bench
ThursdayWalk 20–30 minutesTandem stance while cleaning your teeth
FridayStrength (as Monday)One-leg stand at the kettle
SaturdayBalance (as Wednesday) + walking with head turnsTake the stairs one extra time
SundayRest, or an easy walkWhatever you can manage

Roughly 2½ hours of structured work, plus the scattered minutes that lift it over the three-hour mark where the benefit is greatest.

The other half of falls prevention

Exercise is the strongest single measure, but it is not the only one — and some popular measures are weaker than people assume.

🌿 Consider Tai Chi as well

Tai Chi reduces falls — by around 19% across the trials, with weaker evidence than the balance programmes above. But one well-run trial of a Tai Chi programme designed specifically for people at high risk of falling outperformed a conventional multimodal exercise class. It is worth adding, particularly if a weekly class is something you would actually attend; it is not a replacement for the strength and balance work.

🏠 Fix the house — properly

Removing hazards reduces falls by around a quarter overall, and by nearly 40% in people already at high risk. What works is an actual assessment and actual changes: rails by the toilet and shower, non-slip mats, better lighting, removing loose rugs and clutter, and a clear night route. A leaflet does not work. If you have fallen, ask about an occupational therapist home visit.

👓 Check your glasses, not just your eyes

Multifocal and bifocal lenses blur the ground just where you need to see it, and impair depth perception at kerbs and stairs. If you are active, a separate pair of single-vision distance glasses for walking outdoors is worth discussing with your optometrist. Have cataracts treated — first-eye surgery reduces falls.

💊 Review the medicines

Sedatives, sleeping tablets, antidepressants, antipsychotics, opioids, some bladder medications, and anything that lowers blood pressure all raise falls risk. So does the combination of several of them. This is worth a formal review with your GP or pharmacist — bring every packet, including the ones you buy yourself.

🩸 Check your blood pressure standing up

A drop in blood pressure on standing is common, treatable, and often missed because it is only found if someone measures lying and then standing. If you feel light-headed, grey out, or feel worse after meals or in the morning, tell me.

👟 Wear proper shoes indoors

Well-fitting shoes with a firm heel counter, a low broad heel and a thin, non-slip sole. Not slippers without backs, not loose scuffs, and not socks on floorboards. Bare feet are fine and better than socks.

🦴 Protect the bone as well as preventing the fall

If you have osteoporosis, or have broken a bone after a minor fall, then treating the bone matters as much as the balance work — a fall you cannot prevent should not cost you a hip. Ask about a bone density scan and about treatment.

Things people believe that are not true

"Vitamin D will stop me falling."

It will not, unless you are actually deficient. In community-dwelling older adults, vitamin D supplements have not been shown to prevent falls or fractures, and large intermittent doses have increased falls in two trials. If you are deficient, house-bound, or have osteoporosis, replacement is still worthwhile — but it is not a falls treatment, and more is not better.

"I walk every day, so my balance is fine."

Walking is excellent for your heart, your mood, your bones and your nerves. But across 88 trials, programmes built around walking had smaller effects on falls than programmes built around balance. Walking trains walking. Balance has to be trained on its own.

"If I use a stick, I'll become dependent on it."

A walking aid used properly lets you do more, not less — and more activity is what protects you. Two walking poles are often better than one stick because they give information on both sides. What matters is that the aid is the right height and that someone has shown you how to use it.

"I'd better sit down more so I don't fall."

This is the most dangerous idea on the page. Reducing activity to avoid falling weakens exactly the muscles that prevent falls, and fear of falling is itself an independent risk factor for falling. The answer to unsteadiness is training it in a safe place, not avoiding it.

"Wobble boards and balance cushions are the proper way to train."

They are clinic tools used with someone standing beside you. At home, alone, the useful equivalents are a folded towel or a firm sofa cushion, used with both hands on the bench — and only once the flat-floor work is easy.

"I've only had one fall — it was just a trip."

Almost every fall is 'just a trip'. A single fall is the strongest predictor of the next one, and it is the point at which the causes are most treatable. Tell me about it.

"A big multi-part falls programme from the hospital would sort this out."

Perhaps less than you would expect. Large multifactorial programmes — assessment of everything, referrals in all directions — have produced disappointing or borderline results in trials, including a very large American study that failed to reduce serious fall injuries. Podiatry packages have likewise come out neutral.

This is not an argument against treating what is treatable. It is an argument for putting your effort where the effect actually is: challenging balance exercise, at enough of a dose, done indefinitely.

If you do fall: the plan you make in advance

Long lies on the floor cause far more harm than the fall itself. Rehearse this before you need it.

1

Do not rush to get up

Lie still for a moment. Check whether anything hurts badly, and whether you can move both arms and both legs. If you suspect a broken bone, or you hit your head, or you are on blood thinners, call for help and stay where you are.

2

Roll, crawl, kneel, rise

Roll onto your side, then onto your hands and knees. Crawl to a solid chair or a bed. Put both hands on the seat, bring your strongest leg up so that foot is flat on the floor, then push up through that leg and both arms and turn to sit.

3

If you cannot get up

Get to a warm place if you can — drag a blanket or cushion down. Keep moving your arms and legs to protect your skin and circulation. Bang on a wall or floor. This is exactly what a personal alarm pendant is for, and why it must be worn rather than left on the bedside table.

4

Tell me about it

Every fall is worth reporting, even one you were not hurt by. A fall is the single strongest predictor of the next fall, and most causes are treatable — blood pressure medication, vision, inner ear, sensation in the feet, or simple loss of leg strength.

Being honest about the evidence: teaching people to get up off the floor is widely recommended on the strength of the harm caused by long lies — about half of uninjured people who fall cannot get up unaided, and pressure injury, dehydration, muscle breakdown, hypothermia and pneumonia all follow from lying there. The trials that have tested floor-rise training are small and have not shown a clear change in the ability to rise. Rehearse it anyway: the cost is five minutes and the plan itself is worth having.
Hurt is not the same as harm

Muscles that have worked will ache. As a rule of thumb, discomfort up to about 4 or 5 out of 10 during and after exercise is acceptable, provided it settles back to your normal level within 24 hours and is not getting worse week on week. Sharp, sudden or one-sided pain is a reason to stop.

Making it actually happen

The best programme is the one you will still be doing in three months. These are the things that reliably make the difference.

🔗 Attach it to something you already do

Balance work while the kettle boils. Neck exercises after brushing your teeth. Relaxation practice as you get into bed. A new habit hooked onto an old one survives; a new habit floating free does not.

📅 Keep a tick sheet

A calendar on the fridge with a tick for each day. Self-monitoring is one of the few adherence strategies with consistent evidence behind it, and it gives us something real to look at in clinic.

🎯 Set a specific, checkable goal

Not 'improve my balance', but 'stand on one leg for 30 seconds each side by the end of March', or 'walk to the shops and back without stopping'. Write it down.

⏱️ Ten minutes beats an hour you never start

Short daily sessions beat one long weekly effort. The programmes below are designed to be done in ten to twenty minutes, most days, in your own kitchen or hallway.

Almost every trial that produced a real result ran for at least eight to twelve weeks. Judge the programme at three months, not at three days.

Getting extra help in Australia

You do not have to do this alone, and supervised programmes work better than unsupervised ones for people at higher risk.

🩺 Your GP can subsidise allied health

Since 1 July 2025, GP Management Plans and Team Care Arrangements have been replaced by the GP Chronic Condition Management Plan. With one in place, you can access up to five Medicare-rebated allied health services per calendar year — shared across all disciplines, so five physiotherapy sessions means none left for anything else (ten services for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients). Referral is now by an ordinary letter rather than a special form. Ask your GP whether you are eligible.

🏃 Physiotherapist or exercise physiologist

A physiotherapist is the right choice for a specific problem — a painful neck, an unsteady gait, vestibular rehabilitation. An accredited exercise physiologist is the right choice for building and supervising a long-term conditioning programme. Both can be seen privately without a referral.

👥 Community falls programmes

NSW Health and many local councils run group strength-and-balance programmes such as Stepping On. Group programmes add the two things a home sheet cannot: supervision and company. Ask your GP or your local council, or search Active and Healthy NSW.

🏠 My Aged Care and NDIS

If you are over 65 and finding daily tasks harder, a My Aged Care assessment can fund home exercise support, home modifications such as rails, and an occupational therapy home-safety visit. Under 65 with a permanent disability, the same supports may be available through the NDIS.

Contact me, or your GP, if
  • You have had a fall — any fall, even one where you were not hurt.
  • You are having black-outs, faints, or falls with no warning at all.
  • You feel light-headed on standing, particularly in the morning or after meals.
  • The unsteadiness has come on quickly, over days to weeks, rather than gradually.
  • You have new numbness, weakness, double vision, slurred speech, or spinning vertigo.
  • You are becoming frightened to leave the house because of your balance.
